newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine stocks seen as a better buy than bonds.
newsitem.headline: Argentine stocks seen as a better buy than bonds.

text.p: The time for switching out of Argentine bonds and into stocks is drawing nearer and not only because of cyclical factors, analysts say.
"It is a (bond) market for switching out of, and into stocks. There is a lot more equity potential now," said Peter Schubert, an analyst at Interacciones brokers.

Bonds have outperformed this year. According to the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Composite Index, Argentine bonds have risen 22.9 percent in the year to date compared with a rise of 16.3 percent in the blue chip MerVal .MERV stock index.
But that trend should be reversed now that there are clear signs of a rebound in growth. Schubert forecasts the MerVal will rise to 750 index points in the course of next year from its current 617.

"We see stocks as a better buy than bonds basically because the improvements in economic activity are not reflected in company balance sheets," said Luis Secco, chief economist at consultants Broda y Asociados.

For instance, industrial production has steadily risen this year, culminating in year-on-year increases of 11.3 percent in October and 9.2 percent in September, according to data from the FIEL private consultancy.

Gross domestic product could grow more than three percent this year after contracting 4.6 percent last year in the wake of the tequila crisis in 1995. The government and some analysts think GDP could could grow five percent next year.

Even if this growth helps improve the budget deficit and thus supports bonds, analysts point out that large debt servicing costs scheduled for next year will lead to more debt issuance and weigh on bond prices. Secco estimates debt redemptions, amortizations and interest will be $17 billion in 1997, up from around $12 billion this year.

Hernan Ladeuix, a stock analyst at ING Barings, points out that equities were disproportionately hit by the government fiscal package announced in July because it included increases in corporate tax rates. That means that as growth jumps, stocks have greater potential to catch up.
Perhaps the most convincing argument favoring stocks over bonds is the soaring demand for stocks from Argentine pension funds.

The private pension funds, which were established in the middle of 1994, have already increased their portfolio weightings of stocks to 15.7 percent of their funds at the end of October from just 5.9 at the beginning of 1996.

But that is still way below their maximum allowed portfolio weighting in stocks of 35 percent. The funds already have 49.8 percent of their capital invested in Argentine bonds, just below the maximum allowed weighting of 50 percent, meaning the potential for growth in that sector is limited. Bond investments have so far proved to be solid investments.

However, "equities remain the only major asset class in which most pension funds are underexposed. In order for pension funds to increase their current returns, fund managers must turn towards the stock market to capture growth," Caspian Securities argued in a recent report on the funds.

Caspian calculates for the funds just to maintain their current weighting of stocks, they will fuel $25 million worth of funds into the equity market every month. If the funds raise their holdings to the maximum level, it would raise their stock investments to $1.1 billion from thei current $735 million.

Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said in a report that the increasing interest in stocks by pension funds will help raise the liquidity of the stock market which in itself may attract more funds from other investors to stocks.

As the pension fund supervisory body eases the regulations on the stocks funds can buy, it may make the stock market even more attractive as "any improvement in the fundamentals of an approved second-tier stock would likely generate great interest among fund managers, causing upward pressure on the stock," said Caspian.
